Hook: In 1914 an economist at Columbia University, Henry Moore, did something new. He took the actual prices and quantities of goods, year by year, and fitted lines through them, which he called statistical laws of demand. For crops like corn and potatoes, his lines sloped down, as demand curves should. For pig iron, the raw material of steel, his line sloped up. Moore didn't flinch. Unlike the law of demand for the crops, he wrote, the law of demand for a producers' good is such that as the supply increases the price rises. A new kind of demand curve, discovered in the data.

A year later an economist named Philip Wright reviewed Moore's book and saw the trouble. Rain moves the supply of crops, so a crop's prices and quantities slide along its demand curve. But the same weather, through the whole state of business, moves the demand for pig iron, so iron's points slide along its supply curve. Moore's upward-sloping law of demand was a supply curve. The data had answered a different question from the one he asked.

The Island can make the same mistake. Here is a season of the fish market, two hundred and forty days, each dot one day's price and the number of fish sold. Put the best straight line through them, and it slopes upward: about 8 more fish sold for every dollar on the price. Do the islanders want more fish when fish is dearer? Of course not. In 1927 an agricultural economist, Elmer Working, asked the question in its general form: what do statistical demand curves show? The answer turned out to be the foundation of modern empirical economics.

This part is about one question: when can data answer an economic question? When does a cloud of prices and quantities tell you about demand? When can you tell whether a programme worked, rather than that the people in it were different? And when will a pattern found in the past survive a government that tries to use it?
Economics, Built. Part four: the evidence.

Part four: the evidence. You'll try to find the demand curve in the Island's cloud, and see why the obvious line fails. Then the fix that Philip Wright found in 1928: an instrument, something like the weather that moves one curve and not the other. We'll meet omitted variables and self-selection, and a famous test in which the methods of the day were checked against an experiment. Then the credibility revolution: draft lotteries, birthdays, state borders and experiments in the field. And we'll finish with the Lucas critique, the argument between structure and design, and what a year of school is worth.
PlayIt: Chapter one. Play it: find the demand curve.

Your turn. Here is the season again: every dot a day. Four lines go through the middle of the cloud. A is the line that fits the dots best. B is steep: buyers who hardly respond to the price. C is in between. D is flat: buyers who respond a great deal. One of them is the islanders' true demand for fish: we planted it, so there is a right answer. Which one? And before you answer, ask yourself: what in the picture could tell you? Pause, and pick.

Here is the truth. The islanders' demand is line C: every dollar on the price costs about 67 fish a day. And here is the supply curve we planted, sloping up. The line that fits the dots best, A, is neither. If you chose C, you were lucky, or you guessed what a demand curve usually looks like. Nothing in the cloud could have told you. The same dots could have come from a steep demand curve, or a flat one, if the curves had moved differently. To find out which, you need to know why the dots are where they are.
Simultaneity: Chapter two. Two curves, one cloud.

Every day in the market, two lines meet. The islanders' demand, and the fishers' supply. The day's price and catch are where they cross: one dot. On a feast day the islanders want more fish at every price, so demand moves out, and the dot slides up along the supply curve. On a stormy day some boats stay in, supply moves in, and the dot slides up along the demand curve. Some days have both. And every day has small shocks of its own to each curve. The season's cloud is the record of all of this, every dot an intersection, and no dot belongs to either curve alone.

Sort the days by what happened. Here is the average day of each kind: ordinary days, feasts, storms, and the few days with both. Going from the ordinary days to the stormy ones, only supply moved, so the step runs along the demand curve. Going to the feast days, only demand moved, so the step runs along supply. A line fitted to all the days mixes the two steps, and leans toward whichever curve moved less: this season there were more feasts than storms, so the cloud leans like supply.

In symbols, which is what Working wrote in words. Demand and supply are two equations with shocks, u and v. The least-squares slope settles, in a long season, on a weighted mixture of the two curves' slopes, weighted by how much each curve moves. With the Island's planted numbers it comes to about plus fifteen; this season's dots gave plus 8. If only demand moved, the cloud would trace supply; if only supply moved, it would trace demand. Since both move, it traces nothing. This is the identification problem, and it is not a problem of too little data. A million more days would give a more precise wrong answer.
Instrument: To find demand, we need days on which only supply moved: something that shifts supply, and has nothing to do with demand. The Island has one: the weather. A storm keeps boats in harbour. It doesn't make anyone hungrier for fish, or less hungry. Colour the season by the weather: 31 stormy days, and the rest calm.

Now compare. On the calm days, the average price and catch sit here. On the stormy days, here: fewer fish, at a higher price. Between the two, only supply has moved, so the step from one to the other runs along the demand curve. Divide the change in the catch by the change in the price, and you have demand's slope: about 65 fish for every dollar. The planted truth is 66.7. The storm has done what no amount of data could: it separated the curves. This ratio is the Wald estimator, and the storm is called an instrument. It works on two conditions. It must move the price, which it does: a storm adds about 56 cents to the price of fish. And it must have no other route to the catch, except through supply. That second condition can't be checked in the data. It's an argument about the world.

The idea is almost a hundred years old. In 1928 Philip Wright published a book on the tariff on animal and vegetable oils, and at the back of it, in Appendix B, he solved Moore's problem. To find the demand for butter and for flaxseed, he used factors that move one curve and not the other, such as the weather where the crop was grown. It was the first instrumental variable estimator. The picture he had in mind was this: the weather has an arrow into supply, supply and demand together make the price and quantity, and there is no arrow from the weather to demand. For decades people wondered whether the appendix was really written by his son, Sewall Wright, a famous geneticist who had invented a method of drawing just such arrows. In 2003 James Stock and Francesco Trebbi compared its style with both men's writing, and concluded it was the father's.

The same trick finds the other curve. Feasts move the islanders' demand and do nothing to the boats. So the step from ordinary days to feast days runs along supply, and its slope is about 90 fish per dollar, against a planted 89. Each curve needs its own instrument: something that moves the other curve, and only the other curve.
Selection: Chapter five. Omitted variables and selection.

The same problem has a second form, and it's everywhere. Here are the Island's school records: every islander's years of schooling and earnings. The best line says each extra year of school goes with about 10 percent higher earnings. Is that what a year of school does? Ask who stays in school longer. On the Island, as everywhere, it's partly the able: the ones who find school easier, and who would earn more whatever their schooling. Colour each islander by ability, which we planted and the statistician can't see, and the able sit high and to the right. Part of the line is ability, not school.

The size of the mistake has a formula, the omitted-variable bias. Suppose earnings depend on schooling and on ability. Leave ability out, and the schooling coefficient picks up ability's effect, times how strongly ability and schooling move together. With the Island's numbers, the line should overstate the return by almost three points. This sample's line says 0.101; the planted return is 0.08. If we could measure ability and hold it fixed, the bias would go. But ability is exactly what we can't measure.

An instrument can rescue us here too. Twenty years ago the Island built a second school, on its east side. Islanders who grew up near it stayed in school about two years longer than those across the Island, 2.0 years on average. And their earnings are higher, by 0.161 in logs. Divide one by the other: 0.080, almost exactly the planted eight percent. It works because where the school was built changed how much schooling islanders could get, and nothing about how able they were. That, again, is an argument, not a fact in the data. Real studies have used distance to a college, changes in the school-leaving age and new school buildings in exactly this way.

The deepest form of the problem is choice. Think of a training programme for the unemployed. Who signs up? People whose earnings have just dropped: Orley Ashenfelter noticed in 1978 that trainees' earnings dip in the year before they enrol, and recover afterwards whether or not the training helped. People who expect to gain the most. And people with less going for them to begin with. Compare trainees with everyone else, and you're comparing different people. Economists in the 1970s had a toolkit of regressions and corrections for exactly this. The next chapter is the test of that toolkit.
LaLonde: Chapter six. The con, and LaLonde's test.

By the early 1980s many economists had lost faith in their own regressions. In 1983 Edward Leamer of UCLA published an article called Let's Take the Con out of Econometrics. Hardly anyone takes data analyses seriously, he wrote. Or perhaps more accurately, hardly anyone takes anyone else's data analyses seriously. His complaint was that results depended on which controls the researcher chose to include, and researchers reported only the specifications they liked: like elaborately plumed birds, he wrote, we preen and strut and display our t-values.

Three years later came the test. In the mid-1970s the United States ran a training programme called the National Supported Work Demonstration, which guaranteed hard-to-employ workers a job for nine to eighteen months, working in small crews. And it was run as an experiment: applicants were assigned by lottery, so those who got the programme and those who didn't were alike in every way but one. For men, the programme raised 1978 earnings by 886 dollars, in the dollars of 1982. Robert LaLonde, a young economist, asked a devastating question. Suppose there had been no lottery. Suppose an evaluator had compared the trainees with men from the big national surveys, as evaluators normally did, and applied the methods of the day. Would they have found the answer?

Here is the answer, from his table for the men. The dashed line is the truth the experiment found. Compare the trainees with men from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, and the programme seems to have cut their earnings by 15,578 dollars: the trainees were simply poorer to begin with. Adjust by regression for age, schooling and race, and it still cuts them by 8,067. The other methods of the day scatter around the truth, some near it, some thousands of dollars away, with comparison groups from the census's survey just as bad. Worse, LaLonde found that the standard specification tests couldn't tell the good estimates from the bad. Without the experiment, an honest evaluator would not have known which number to believe.

The story has a sequel. In 1999 Rajeev Dehejia and Sadek Wahba went back to LaLonde's data. Here are the trainees, the lottery losers and a group of survey men, in the subsample they used. The trainees and the lottery losers look alike. The survey men are older, far more often married, and earned more than twice as much before the programme. In this subsample the experiment says the programme added about 1,800 dollars. The raw comparison with the survey men gets even the sign wrong. But compare like with like, holding past earnings fixed, and the estimate comes close: about 1,500. So careful methods can work. The catch is the one LaLonde found: we only know this one worked because the experiment was there to check it.

Called it? The series keeps score of predictions, and this one is clear. The standard evaluation of the day said the programme cut men's earnings by about eight thousand dollars. The lottery said it raised them by about nine hundred. Wrong, and wrong in sign. What came next was a change of strategy. If experiments give answers that regressions can't, then find the experiments: the lotteries, accidents and rules that the world runs anyway.
Experiments: Why does a lottery work when careful regressions fail? Watch it on the Island. The boatwrights offer a year's apprenticeship, and we've planted its effect: it raises a young islander's earnings by ten percent. First, let the islanders choose. Those with the poorest prospects are keenest to sign up. Here is their ability, which we planted and nobody can see: the ones who signed up sit to the left of the ones who stayed out. Compare their earnings, and the apprenticeship seems to cut them, by 15 percent. Wrong in sign, like the survey comparisons in LaLonde's test. Now give the places by lottery. The winners and the losers are alike in ability, not because anyone measured it, but because a coin can't tell who is able. And the gap in earnings is 11 percent, within its margin of the truth. That is what randomization buys: balance on everything, including what no one can see.

Economists began running such lotteries on purpose in the late 1960s, on the biggest question in welfare policy. Milton Friedman had proposed a negative income tax: give every family a guaranteed income, and as the family earns more, take back part of each dollar, until at the break-even point the payment runs out. The worry was obvious. If each dollar you earn keeps only fifty cents, will you work less? Nobody's regressions could settle it. So from 1968 about thirteen hundred and fifty low-income families in New Jersey and Pennsylvania were assigned at random to eight different plans, or to none, with guarantees from half the poverty line to one and a quarter times it, and tax rates of thirty, fifty or seventy percent. Larger trials followed, the biggest in Seattle and Denver. Their answer: people did work somewhat less, husbands a little, wives and single mothers more. Some of the fall turned out to be earnings that families simply didn't report, which is its own lesson in measurement.

The idea travelled. In 1997 Mexico launched PROGRESA, which paid mothers in poor rural villages if their children went to school and the family kept its visits to the clinic. Its designer, the economist Santiago Levy, then deputy finance minister, wanted proof that would outlast the government. Five hundred and six villages were chosen for the evaluation. There wasn't money to start everywhere at once, so a lottery decided the order: three hundred and twenty villages began first, and the other one hundred and eighty-six about two years later. The comparison was clean. Enrolment rose, most at the step from primary into secondary school, and most for girls. When a new government took office, the programme survived under a new name, and versions of it now run in dozens of countries.

Experiments in economics now come in four kinds. In the laboratory, people trade and bargain for real money: Vernon Smith's double auctions, which you saw in Part 2, won him a Nobel prize in 2002. In the field, experiments run in real markets, with the people who trade there, sometimes without their knowing they are in one. Policy trials test programmes before they are scaled up: textbooks and deworming pills in Kenyan schools, microcredit in Indian cities. Michael Kremer, Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo shared the 2019 prize for this approach. And inside online firms, thousands of small experiments run every day; chapter twelve meets the people who run them. But an experiment has a limit built in. It answers the question it asked, in the place and time it asked it. Whether the answer travels is a different question, and the next two chapters are about it.
Lucas: The last warning in this part is about time. Through the 1960s, American unemployment and inflation moved like a seesaw: as unemployment fell, year by year, inflation rose. In 1960 Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow had called such a curve a menu of choice: pick less unemployment, and pay for it in inflation. Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued that the menu would vanish as soon as anyone ordered from it. Once people came to expect the inflation, they'd build it into their wages and prices, and it would buy nothing. The 1970s proved them right. Inflation and unemployment rose together. Part 28 tells that story in full. Here the question is what it means for evidence.

Here is the same thing on the Island, where we know the rules. For thirty years the Island's council left inflation to chance. In years when prices rose faster than people expected, fishers mistook higher prices for better demand and worked harder, so output rose. Collect the thirty years, and a statistician finds a reliable pattern: each point of inflation goes with 0.86 points of extra output. The council reads this as a menu. Hold inflation at 8 percent, and output should reach 105. So it tries. The first year works: output jumps. Then it falls back, year after year, to where it started. The reason is in people's heads. The islanders learn to expect eight percent, and once they expect it, it fools no one. Nothing in the thirty calm years was wrong. The pattern was real. It just described how people behaved under one policy, and the council changed the policy.

In 1976 Robert Lucas turned this into a principle that changed macroeconomics. The relations in an econometric model, he argued, are summaries of people's decisions; their decisions depend on the policies they expect; so any change in policy will systematically alter the structure of econometric models. What moves are the patterns that summarize behaviour under one policy. What may stay put are the things underneath: what people want, what technology allows, how they form their expectations. Haavelmo had a word for relations that survive a change of regime: autonomous. The search for them is the subject of the next chapter.
Dials: Chapter eleven. The Dials: what is a year of school worth?

This part enters a second dial: the return to a year of school, the proportional rise in earnings it brings. Its estimates come from natural experiments, each set beside the plain regression on the same data, as David Card collected them in 2001. Angrist and Krueger's three cohorts, with quarter of birth, and Staiger and Stock's sharper version. Tuition and distance to college for American women; a four-year college nearby for American men; growing up in a Finnish university town. Britain's changes in the school-leaving age; a programme for Canadian veterans; distance to school in the rural Philippines; and Indonesia's great school-building programme of the 1970s, studied by Esther Duflo. Look at the squares and the dots. The regressions cluster between five and nine percent. The natural experiments spread wider, and in 9 studies of 11 they sit above the regression on the same data.

Some instruments in that table are weak: they move schooling only a little. In 1995 John Bound, David Jaeger and Regina Baker showed why that matters with a startling experiment. They replaced the real quarters of birth with random ones, and got estimates much like the published ones. Try it on the Island. Take 60 instruments of pure noise, coin flips with nothing to do with schooling or pay, and run two-stage least squares. Do it 400 times. The estimates don't scatter around zero. They pile up around the least-squares answer, bias and all. With many weak instruments, the first stage fits noise, and the noise brings the endogeneity back in. The real instrument, the new school, gives 0.080, and its first stage is strong. Douglas Staiger and James Stock's rule of thumb followed: report the first-stage F statistic, and worry when it is below about ten.

Why would the natural experiments find more than the regressions, when we feared the regressions were too high? Card weighed several explanations. Here are four. The ability bias may simply be small. Reported schooling contains errors, and errors pull least squares down, offsetting the ability bias. The people an instrument moves, those who'd have left school early without a college nearby or a stricter law, may gain more from a year than the average person: Imbens and Angrist's local effect, at work. And journals may favour large, significant estimates: Orley Ashenfelter and his coauthors found signs of exactly that. The dial's status is settled within a range. A year of school raises earnings by something like six to fifteen percent, a return few investments match. Part 38 comes back to it.
Practice: Chapter twelve. In practice: who evaluates for a living.

Who does this for a living? Evaluation firms. MDRC was founded in 1974 to run the Supported Work demonstration, the experiment behind LaLonde's test, and firms like it still run many of the government's trials. Development labs such as J-PAL and Innovations for Poverty Action, which have run field trials in dozens of countries. Evaluation offices inside governments, which ask whether a programme is worth its budget. Experimentation teams at online firms, running thousands of controlled experiments a year, on platforms built to stop engineers from stopping a test the moment it looks good. Expert witnesses, whose regressions are cross-examined in discrimination, antitrust and damages cases. And researchers at central banks, who must identify the effect of an interest-rate change when every change is a deliberate choice. Part 55 is theirs.

Here is how a trial is planned, step by step. First the question, and the one number that will answer it. The effect of offering the apprenticeship is not the effect of taking it up, and the plan must say which. Then the size: enough people to see the effect if it's there. Then a plan written and registered before any data arrive: the outcome, the comparison, the controls. Since 2013 economists register their trials with the American Economic Association. Leamer's complaint was about choices made after seeing the data; a plan takes them away. Randomize, and check that the groups are alike on everything measured beforehand. Run it, and count who drops out: if the losers of the lottery leave more often than the winners, the lottery is broken again. And analyse as planned, reporting every outcome, the dull ones included.

The second step deserves a picture. The smallest effect a trial can reliably detect shrinks with the square root of its size. Reliably means: with a five percent false-alarm rate, it finds a real effect of that size four times in five. On the Island, earnings vary with a spread of about 0.39 in logs, and half the people are offered the apprenticeship. To detect its planted ten percent you need about 480 islanders. With four hundred, a simulation finds it 71 times in a hundred. With the sixteen hundred we used, almost always. The square root is a hard master: to see an effect half the size, you need four times as many people. Many published trials were too small to see the effects they were looking for, which is one reason their findings so often fail to repeat.
Frontier: Chapter thirteen. Frontier: when treatments spill over.

Every design in this part rests on an assumption so natural that it's easy to miss: one person's treatment doesn't change anyone else's outcome. In a market it often fails. Take the Island's apprenticeship again, and suppose every apprentice takes a little of the boatwrights' work from the other young islanders in the same village. Run the trial in 100 villages, and let a lottery decide not just who gets a place, but what share of each village does: none, a quarter, a half, three quarters or all. Inside each village, those offered a place earn about ten percent more than their neighbours. That's what an ordinary trial would report. But look across villages. The more of a village is offered a place, the less everyone in it earns, including those who weren't. So the effect of the policy, a place for everyone against a place for no one, is a small fraction of what the trial said. The gain was partly taken from the neighbours.

The best evidence now comes from trials that randomize the share treated, as we just did. In France, Bruno Crépon, Esther Duflo and their coauthors offered job counselling to young job seekers, with the share offered drawn at random across two hundred and thirty-five labour markets. Those offered help found stable jobs sooner, but partly at the expense of those who weren't, and the net gain was small. In Kenya, Dennis Egger and his coauthors followed cash transfers of about a thousand dollars to more than ten thousand households in 653 villages. Each dollar raised local spending and income by about two and a half, with little inflation. In India, Karthik Muralidharan, Paul Niehaus and Sandip Sukhtankar found that a better-run job guarantee raised the earnings of poor households by about fourteen percent, mostly through higher wages in private jobs, not through the programme itself. So the spillover can shrink an effect, multiply it, or be most of it. A trial that can't see it can't tell you which.

What is not known? Above all, when the effect a trial finds will survive being scaled to a whole market, and how to tell before spending the money. The statistics are being built: designs that randomize at two levels, as in Michael Hudgens and Elizabeth Halloran's work, and Peter Aronow and Cyrus Samii's exposure mappings, which say exactly which neighbours' treatments can reach you. The same problem now costs online platforms money every day: when buyers and sellers share a market, a test on some of them changes the market for the rest. And here is the research problem for this part. Design the Island's next trial: how many villages, at what shares, to detect a spillover half the size of this one? The problem set has the place to start.
